## Concepts and intuitions {.unnumbered}



## Formal {.unnumbered}
In theoretical mathematical statistics, a statistic has a very precise mathematical definition. It is not just a descriptive number, but a function mapping a sample of random variables to a new random variable or vector. Crucially, a function is only a statistic if it does not depend on any unknown parameters.
Here are the rigorous definitions from two of the most widely used advanced textbooks in mathematical statistics, along with their raw LaTeX representations.

1. The Standard Mathematical Statistics Definition
This definition establishes a statistic as a real-valued or vector-valued function of the sample data that remains completely observable.

Textbook Source
Book: Statistical Inference (2nd Edition, 2002)
Authors: George Casella and Roger L. Berger
Publisher: Duxbury / Thomson Learning
The Definition

In Chapter 5 ("Properties of a Random Sample"), Casella and Berger define a statistic as follows:
Definition 5.2.1: "Let X1,…,Xn be a random sample of size n from a population. A statistic is a real-valued or vector-valued function of the sample, $T(X_1, \dots, X_n)$."

They explicitly append a vital mathematical caveat immediately following the definition:
"Note that a statistic is a random variable (or a random vector). [...] The definition of a statistic states that a statistic is a function of the sample only. In particular, a function that depends on an unknown parameter cannot be a statistic."

2. The Measure-Theoretic Definition
In graduate-level statistics, the sample data is treated as an element of a sample space, and the statistic is defined strictly as a measurable mapping that abstracts the data.

Textbook Source
Book: Mathematical Statistics (2nd Edition, 2003)
Author: Jun Shao
Publisher: Springer Science & Business Media

The Definition
In Chapter 2 ("Fundamentals of Estimation"), Shao formalizes a statistic using measure theory:
"A measurable function of the data X, say T(X), is called a statistic if T(X) does not depend on the unknown parameter θ. The range of T(X) is a subset of Rk $T(X) \in \mathbb{R}^k$ for some integer k≥1."
He further notes that if T(X) is used to estimate θ, it is called an estimator, but its underlying mathematical classification remains a statistic.

3. Visualizing a Statistic as a Function

To understand this concept intuitively, a statistic acts as a mathematical bridge that collapses a high-dimensional dataset down into a single summary measure:
Core Structural Requirements of a Statistic
As outlined in these texts, for any expression to be rigorously classified as a statistic, it must pass two mathematical tests:
Parameter Independence: It cannot contain unknown population terms.
Is a Statistic: The sample mean
$\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$. You can compute this number directly from your data.

Is NOT a Statistic: The standardizing formula
$Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}$ (where μ is an unknown population mean). Because you do not know μ, you cannot compute Z directly from the sample alone; it is *a pivotal quantity*, not a statistic.
It is a Random Variable: Because the sample observations X1,…,Xn
​ are random variables, any function T(⋅) applied to them is itself a random variable. Consequently, a statistic always possesses its own probability distribution, rigorously known as its sampling distribution.
